question: to the Commission Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Antonín Staněk (PfE), Pierre Pimpie (PfE), Marion Maréchal (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Fernand Kartheiser (NI), Nikola Bartůšek (NI) Subject:

The Commission has added a policy debate on revising the merger control guidelines to the agenda for the meeting of the College of Commissioners on 18 March 20261. Against a backdrop of heightened international competition, many consider the EU framework overly restrictive. While it is essential to stamp out ‘killer acquisitions’, particularly by firms from outside the EU, a number of innovative start-ups, including digital start-ups, have voiced concerns about a possible tightening of the acquisition framework. A disproportionate and insufficiently predictable approach, based on purely speculative competition scenarios, could impinge on the exit prospects at the heart of the venture capital and private equity models on which these companies may be based. In light of this: 1.
How will the Commission strike a balance between preventing killer acquisitions and ensuring greater predictability and proportionality in merger control, particularly for innovative start-ups?

Does it intend to adjust certain parameters within the merger control framework, such as notification thresholds or the assessment criteria for non-horizontal mergers, in order to promote the growth and competitiveness of EU companies, particularly in strategic technology sectors?
https://www.contexte.com/medias/pdf/medias-documents/2026/2/lpp-17-fevrier.pdf.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.5.2026) The main goal of the Merger Guidelines revision is to modernise EU merger policy. Mergers can have positive and negative effects for the competitiveness of the EU economy. Through this revision the Commission will provide a clear and modern assessment framework so that companies, of all sizes, have the necessary predictability when engaging in mergers. Importantly, the revised Guidelines will include positive guidance on which acquisitions involving start-ups are pro-competitive and do not warrant intervention. This ‘innovation shield’ will provide predictability and legal certainty for smaller companies when considering exit strategies. The revised Guidelines will also include clear and concrete guidance on those rare acquisitions of nascent or small innovative companies that can instead stifle innovation and merit intervention. It is critical to prevent killer acquisitions. Therefore, the Commission supports Member States’ efforts to review such mergers and will consider appropriate referrals under Article 22 of the EU Merger Regulation referred by competent Member States. The Commission will not adjust the merger control notification thresholds since the EU Merger Regulation is not subject to review. The revised Merger Guidelines will instead provide updated guidance on the Commission’s assessment criteria for all mergers, including non-horizontal ones. The fundamental objective of merger control will not change: preventing harmful mergers that lead to too much market power in the hands of too few companies – harming innovation and growth. However, there will be new guidance on pro-competitive scale and a new framework to assess dynamic efficiencies that may be pertinent to mergers in strategic technology sectors.
